summary: A candidate whom Pindrop calls “Ivan X” applied for a remote engineering role and advanced from résumé screening to a video interview on 18 February 2025. Pindrop said the candidate’s video showed unnatural facial movements and audio lag, and its detection tool flagged a face swap. Pindrop described a second interview eight days later under the same identity with a different apparent face. The company identified the application as fraudulent; the available account does not say Ivan X was hired or passed its interview identity check.

assessment_boundaries: Pindrop’s account is first-party reporting by the targeted company; raw interview material and its detection telemetry were not independently tested here.
Advancement to interview and a later coding assessment do not establish that identity checks were passed or that employment was offered.
The Guardian article covers a broader pattern, not additional consequences caused by Ivan X.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The AI Incident Database entry identifies an attempted deepfake job application at Pindrop. Pindrop’s first-party account places Ivan X in an interview, describes visible anomalies and says its tool confirmed the suspected face swap. A later Pindrop account says the screening interview was on 18 February 2025 and its real-time assistant flagged the video; it also reports a subsequent coding assessment, which should not be mistaken for verified identity or hiring. The Guardian article concerns a wider pattern of AI-assisted remote hiring and does not prove a different outcome for Ivan X. No employment, payroll access or downstream compromise is established. Pindrop’s 18 June 2025 retrospective confirms that the role was a remote engineering job, that the synthetic video was presented during the 18 February screening interview, and that its assistant flagged the face swap. This was a bid for paid employment, although neither a job offer nor a wage transfer is reported.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The human-directed applicant used an AI-mediated false visual presentation to seek a paid engineering role. The attempted employment decision had a materially misleading identity premise even though Pindrop detected the face swap during interview and reports no hire. Detection preserves the identity-verification boundary in the observed process; it does not erase the attempted deceptive economic solicitation. The record does not attribute the applicant’s objective or tactic selection to the AI system, or infer a generator-side consent failure.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: A face-swapped candidate presentation can be part of a false economic premise in an attempted paid hiring decision. Pindrop’s detection prevented the available record from establishing a completed hire; the attempted solicitation and successful interview-stage detection are separate governance facts.
